title: Confession, a Sliding Scale, and the Guilt Offering
summary: The first half of the chapter continues the sin offering with specific failures: keeping silent when called to testify, touching something unclean, and swearing a thoughtless oath. The offender must confess, and the offering is scaled to what he can afford, from a lamb or goat down to two birds or a little flour. The second half introduces the guilt offering, a ram brought with repayment plus a fifth by someone who has misused the LORD's holy things or suspects he has sinned without knowing it.
story: Chapter 4 set out the sin offering by the rank of the person who sinned. Chapter 5 keeps the same offering but turns to particular situations that ordinary Israelites would meet, and it adds something chapter 4 did not state: the sinner must say out loud what he has done (verse 5). Then a new speech from the LORD (verse 14) introduces the last of the five main offerings, the guilt offering, which deals with wrongs that can be measured and repaid. It continues into 6:1-7, where the wrong is done to a neighbor rather than to God's property. With that, the section of Leviticus written from the worshiper's side of the altar is complete, and 6:8 begins the same offerings again from the priests' side. The guilt offering will reappear when a person healed of skin disease is restored (14:12), when a Nazirite's vow is broken by contact with a corpse (Numbers 6:12), and in Isaiah's portrait of a servant whose life is made a guilt offering (Isaiah 53:10).
historical:
Verse 1 refers to a legal practice common in the ancient world. When a crime had no known witness, the victim or the court could pronounce a public curse (Hebrew alah) on anyone who knew the facts and kept silent. In Judges 17:2 a mother utters such a curse over eleven hundred shekels of silver stolen from her, and the thief, her own son, confesses. Proverbs 29:24 describes the accomplice who “receives the oath, but does not testify.” Leviticus treats such silence as a sin that needs confession and an offering, because justice in a village depended on people telling what they had seen.

The guilt offering's ram is valued “in silver shekels according to the sanctuary shekel” (verse 15). The shekel was a weight of silver, commonly estimated at a little over 11 grams, not yet a coin; coinage first appeared in Lydia in western Asia Minor around the seventh century BC. The sanctuary shekel was a standard weight of twenty gerahs (Exodus 30:13), which protected both worshiper and priest from dishonest scales. The idea of reparation for offending a deity reached beyond Israel. When the Philistines returned the captured ark, their priests told them to send it back “with a guilt offering” of gold objects (1 Samuel 6:3), using this same Hebrew word.
cultural:
The sliding scale in verses 7-13 reflects real poverty. A lamb or young goat was a significant part of a poor family's wealth. Turtledoves and young pigeons were cheap, since they could be caught wild or kept around the house, and the priest killed them by twisting the head at the neck. For those who could not manage even birds, a tenth of an ephah of fine flour (commonly estimated at around two liters) would do. The flour carried no oil or frankincense, the additions that accompanied the grain offering of chapter 2, because this was an offering for sin and not a gift of devotion. The priest burned a handful on the altar on top of the other offerings, so that even the poorest person's offering was joined to the altar where blood atonement was made.

The holy things of verse 15 are whatever belonged to God: sacrifices, the priests' portions, tithes, firstfruits, and dedicated gifts (compare 22:14 and 27:30). To misuse them, for example by eating a priest's portion or keeping back a tithe, was a breach of trust against God himself. The remedy was concrete. The offender repaid the value, added a fifth, and brought a ram. Forgiveness in this system did not skip repayment; it came through it.
literary: The chapter has two parts marked by the formula “Then the LORD said to Moses” at verse 14. Verses 1-4 list four cases. In the first a witness keeps silent; in the other three the person is unaware at first and only later realizes his guilt. Verses 5-13 give the remedy, beginning with confession and then descending in cost, from a flock animal (verse 6) to birds (7-10) to flour (11-13), with the same promise at each level: he will be forgiven. Verses 14-19 introduce the guilt offering in two cases: sacrilege against holy things (14-16) and sin that the offender suspects but cannot identify (17-19). The Hebrew root asham, to be guilty, runs through both halves, sometimes meaning to be guilty, sometimes the penalty owed, and sometimes the guilt offering itself, so English versions must choose different words for it; in verses 6 and 7 the BSB renders it as guilt offering and restitution. In Hebrew Bibles this chapter runs on for seven more verses, which English Bibles number 6:1-7.

outline.t: Silence, contact with uncleanness, and rash oaths
Confession and a sin offering from the flock
For those who cannot afford a lamb: two birds
For those who cannot afford birds: fine flour
The guilt offering for misusing holy things
The guilt offering for sin unknowingly committed

doctrines.note: Verse 5 requires the offender to confess the specific sin he has committed. The offering is not a way around admitting the wrong; it follows the admission. The guilt offering adds repayment, so repentance here includes both words and restitution.

The descending scale shows that atonement was never meant to be a privilege of the wealthy. The poorest Israelite with a handful of flour received the same promise as the owner of a flock: the priest will make atonement, and he will be forgiven.

Some things belong to God in a special way, and treating them as ordinary is a real offense against him. The guilt offering teaches that holiness has an economic side: what has been taken from God must be given back, with interest.

words.note: Asham, guilt offering. The noun can mean guilt, the penalty owed for it, or the offering that repairs it. Because the offering always involves making good a loss, many scholars call it the reparation offering. The word appears in Isaiah 53:10, where the servant's life is made a guilt offering.

Maal, unfaithfulness or breach of trust. It describes betrayal by someone who owes loyalty, used elsewhere of marital infidelity and of Israel's idolatry. Here it names sacrilege, the misuse of what belongs to God. The same word describes cheating a neighbor in 6:2, since that too is unfaithfulness against the LORD.

Yadah, here in a form meaning to confess (verse 5). The same root elsewhere means to praise or give thanks, as in the thanksgiving psalms. Both senses involve acknowledging something openly before God, whether his goodness or one's own sin.

christ: Isaiah 53 describes a servant of the LORD who suffers for the sins of others, and says that “His soul is made a guilt offering” (Isaiah 53:10). The New Testament repeatedly identifies that servant with Jesus, and when Jesus says he came “to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45), many scholars hear an echo of the same chapter. The guilt offering's logic, that a wrong must be repaid in full before the relationship is whole, helps explain why the New Testament describes Christ's death as paying a debt. The chapter's sliding scale also anticipates the gospel's reach. Hebrews says that under the law “nearly everything must be purified with blood” (Hebrews 9:22), a careful word that leaves room for the flour offering of verses 11-13. The offer of forgiveness never depended on the worshiper's wealth, and in Christ it rests on a sacrifice no one could afford and everyone may receive. And the confession required in verse 5 is echoed in the promise, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

hard.q: How can someone be guilty of a sin he did not know he committed (verses 17-19)?
hard.a:
Modern readers tend to tie guilt to intention, so the idea of being guilty without knowing it can seem unjust. Leviticus works with a wider idea of guilt, closer to what law calls liability: a wrong can be real and cause real damage whether or not the person meant it or noticed it. A driver who backs into a neighbor's fence without noticing is still responsible once he learns of it.

Interpreters read verses 17-19 in two main ways. One view takes the Hebrew as describing objective guilt; the offender has in fact broken a command and must deal with it once he suspects it. Another, argued by Jacob Milgrom, reads the key verb as to feel guilty, describing someone whose conscience troubles him, perhaps because of misfortune, though he cannot name any wrong. On that reading the offering meets a very human need, giving an anxious person a way to put the matter before God and hear that he is forgiven. Either way the text takes hidden sin seriously and also refuses to leave a person without remedy. A psalmist prayed the same way: “Who can discern his own errors? Cleanse me from my hidden faults” (Psalm 19:12).

questions: Verse 1 treats silence as sin when someone knows the truth that would bring justice. Where might keeping quiet be a failure of love for a neighbor?
The guilt offering required paying back what was taken, plus a fifth. Why is an apology without repair often not enough?
The law made sure the poorest person could be forgiven. What in your church's life might quietly make grace feel available only to people who can afford it?
